He sees “the god’s infinite form with many mouths, eyes, arms, thighs, feet, stomachs, and many fearful tusks.” He sees warriors, all the kings and all creatures are entering the god’s blazing mouths from all sides, “rush to their destruction like moths into a flame.” Frightened Arjuna asks this “terrible”…

Here is one of the translated versions after the prince asked “who are you”: “I am death, the mighty destroyer of the world. I have come here to destroy all these people. Even without your participation in the war, all the warriors standing arrayed in the opposing armies shall cease to exist. Therefore get up and attain glory. Conquer your enemies, and enjoy a prosperous kingdom. All these warriors have already been destroyed by Me. You are a mere my instrument... Kill all these great warriors who are already killed by Me. Do not fear. You will certainly conquer the enemies in the battle…

Vishnu was trying to persuade the prince to fight? The nuclear bomb is for sure death and destroyer, but now we realized that the Gita is saying that the people who die in war were already slain by the god, that the warrior was only an instrument. The destruction was decided by Vishnu and Arjuna solely followed his dharma/ duty as a warrior. Did Oppenheimer in some way regard his role in the creation of the atomic bomb as his destined duty, like Arjuna in the war? Did he find solace in this aspect of the Gita’s teachings? That regardless of his participation, the nuclear bomb was inevitable?…

“It was the duty of the scientist to build the bomb, but it was the duty of the statesman to decide how to use it. Oppenheimer clearly and repeatedly acknowledged these very different dharmas.” Despite separating his own dharma/ duty from that of Government leaders, the scientist’s consequential decision deeply tormented him. Throughout the last decades of Oppenheimer's life, he maintained parallel expressions of pride at the technical achievement of the bomb and profound guilt at its devastation. According to Hijiya, Oppenheimer stated more than once that the bomb had simply been inevitable.…

Like it or not, he could not run away from it. Back to the footage with the destroyer quote of the Gita. To me, it not only represents the deadly bomb but also hinted at the inevitability of it and the great dilemma the scientist faced. It doesn’t in any way indicate that Oppenheimer thought there was nuclear war in ancient times. Viewed in this context, the “I am become death” quote possibly reveals how Oppenheimer used philosophy to ease the pain of his conscience. here is how it can be used: “he inspired that blade of grass with proper mantras and converted it into that powerful celestial weapon…he uttered in wrath these terrible words: ‘For the destruction of the Pandavas.’ ...
